'''''Wodyetia''''' is a genus of the palm family [[Arecaceae]], containing the single species '''''Wodyetia bifurcata'''''. The species, commonly known as '''foxtail palm''', is native to a very small area of northeastern [[Queensland]], Australia, but has been widely cultivated around the world.

==Description==
The foxtail palm is a single-stemmed palm growing to a height of {{cvt|6|to|15|m}} tall and up to {{cvt|25|cm}} diameter. The trunk is light grey, smooth (without spines), somewhat bottle- or spindle-shaped, and marked by annular leaf scars. There are about 6–10 fronds in the crown of a mature tree, and they grow to about {{cvt|3|m}} in length with a [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] about {{cvt|90|cm}} long and a {{Botanygloss|sheath|leaf sheath}} about {{cvt|120|cm}} long. The leaflets are divided into numerous segments (as many as 950),{{R|COOPER}} which are arranged radially around the midrib, giving the frond a 'bushy' appearance.{{R|RFK|FOA|IRVINE}}

This species is [[Monoecy|monoecious]],{{R|RIFFLE}} meaning that individual flowers are either {{plantgloss|pistillate flower|pistillate}} (functionally female), or {{plantgloss|staminate flower|staminate}} (functionally male), but both types are produced by each plant. Flowers are carried on a [[panicle]] that emerges from the base of the [[crownshaft]], it may be up to {{cvt|165|cm}} long. Numerous flowers are clustered together in groups of three, each group with one female and two male flowers. They measure about {{cvt|25|mm|0}} diameter (including the petals), and have three yellow-green petals and three green [[sepal]]s.{{R|RFK|FOA|COOPER}}

The fruit is a [[drupe]] up to {{cvt|6.5|cm|1}} long and {{cvt|5|cm|0}} wide, orange-red when ripe. It contains a single large seed coated in a hard but fibrous, black [[mesocarp]].{{R|RFK|FOA|COOPER}}

==Taxonomy==
The foxtail palm was unknown to botanists and horticulturalists as late 1968, when two employees of the Queensland Department of Forestry found it during a survey of the Melville Range. One of the men, [[Bernard Hyland]], returned to the site seven years later and collected the first specimens of the tree.{{R|LA}} In 1982 botanist [[Anthony Kyle Irvine]] also collected specimens from the area, and he set about describing the plant. He created a new genus, ''Wodyetia'', to accommodate the plant, and his work was published in 1983 in the journal of the [[International Palm Society]], ''Principes''.{{R|IRVINE}}

[[File:Foxtail & black palms comparison SF25299 1.jpg|upright=.6|thumb|left|Comparison of flowers and fruit of ''Wodyetia bifurcata'' and ''Normanbya normanbyi'']]
''Wodyetia'' is placed in the subfamily [[Arecoideae]], tribe [[Areceae]], subtribe [[Ptychospermatinae]]. Its nearest relatives include two other [[monotypic taxon|monotypic]] genera that are endemic to Australia, ''[[Carpentaria]]'' and ''[[Normanbya]]''.{{R|BAKER}} The latter is very similar to this taxon, and it has been speculated that ''Wodyetia'' and ''Normanbya'' may be merged into a single genus at some point in the future.{{R|PACSOA}}

===Etymology===
The generic name ''Wodyetia'' is derived from the name of the last [[Aboriginal Australians|aboriginal]] man, Wodyeti, with knowledge of the plants in the Cape Melville area. The [[Botanical name#Binary name|species epithet]] ''bifurcata'' means 'divided in two', and refers to the divided leaflets of the fronds as well as the forked fibres that surround the seed.{{R|COOPER}}

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Cape Melville boulder field.jpg|thumb|The boulder-strewn landscape of Cape Melville]]
This species is endemic to the [[Cape Melville]] range, within the [[Cape Melville National Park (Cape York Peninsula Aboriginal Land)|Cape Melville National Park]] in Queensland Australia. The Park is extremely remote and difficult to access. It is about {{cvt|475|km}} by road north of [[Cairns]], the nearest major population centre, much of that distance is on very challenging unsealed roads.{{R|QPARKS}} 

The foxtail palm grows amongst massive granite boulders on southern slopes of the Cape, in vine thickets with adjacent rainforest. They occur on course sandy soils and are the dominant species within their communities. Co-occurring species include ''[[Buchanania arborescens]]'', ''[[Ficus obliqua]]'', ''[[Ficus benjamina]]'', ''[[Myristica insipida]]'', and climbers such as ''[[Capparis]]'' and ''[[Cissus]]'' species. Near the base of the slopes it grows alongside ''Eucalyptus polycarpa'' (now ''[[Corymbia polycarpa]]''), ''Eucalyptus drepanophylla'' (now ''[[Eucalyptus crebra|E. crebra]]''), ''[[Bombax ceiba]]'' and ''[[Cochlospermum gillivraei]]''. The altitudinal range is small, from near sea level to about {{cvt|400|m}}.{{R|IRVINE|RFK|FOA}}

==Conservation== 
After it was described by Irvine in 1982, the foxtail palm became very much in demand for landscaping. Since it only occurred naturally in a very remote location and was subject to protection laws, a [[Cape Melville incident|thriving black market trade]] arose, with the actions of illegal collectors threatening to ravage native populations.{{R|LA|PACSOA|USBG}} In 1982 Irvine sent seeds to a few horticulturalists in anticipation of, and an attempt to allay, the demand that would follow the publication of this new species. In 1988, a paper was published which cited a [[Brisbane]]-based nursery grower, stating that a single seed was selling in Australia for up to [[Australian dollar|A$]]5,{{R|HULL}} which equates to about $14 in October 2025.{{R|ODF}} In the decades since then, it has been cultivated widely, both in Queensland and around the world, to the point where it is easily and legally available worldwide.{{R|LA|PALMTALK}} {{As of|2025|10}}, more than 1,500 foxtail palms have been planted in the streets and parks of the far northern Queensland city of [[Cairns]].{{R|TREEPLOTTER}}

The [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] (IUCN) last assessed this species in 1998, and gave it a rating of "Lower Risk/conservation dependent". That rating is specified in version 2.3 of the IUCN's rating system, which is now superseded by version 3.1. The IUCN's webpage for the foxtail palm has the annotation 'Needs updating', but does not provide a timeframe for it.{{R|IUCN}} In Queensland, where it is native, the species is assessed as [[near-threatened species|near threatened]] {{As of|2025|10|lc=y}} under the [[Nature Conservation Act 1992]]. It has not been listed in the Australian Government's [[Species Profile and Threats Database]] under the [[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]].{{R|SPRAT}}

==Ecology==
The area has been recognised for its rich [[biocultural diversity]], having long and intense Aboriginal associations and a rich biodiversity.<ref name="QPWS">[http://www.epa.qld.gov.au/parks_and_forests/find_a_park_or_forest/cape_melville_national_park/cape_melville_national_park__nature_culture_and_history/ Queensland National Parks and Wildlife Service's (2008) '''Cape Melville National Park - Nature, culture and history''' webpage] Accessed 4 May 2008 {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080415104738/http://www.epa.qld.gov.au/parks_and_forests/find_a_park_or_forest/cape_melville_national_park/cape_melville_national_park__nature_culture_and_history/ |date=April 15, 2008 }}</ref>
